newsitem.title: USA: Legendary San Francisco columnist Herb Caen dies.
newsitem.headline: Legendary San Francisco columnist Herb Caen dies.

text.p: Herb Caen, a legendary newspaper columnist who wrote about San Francisco life for nearly 60 years, died on Saturday after losing a battle with cancer, the San Francisco Chronicle said. He was 80.
The Pulitzer prize-winning journalist many called "Mr. San Francisco" died early on Saturday at Pacific Medical Centre in the city, the newspaper said in a statement.
Caen broke the news to his readers in May last year that he had inoperable lung cancer. Chronicle Executive Editor Matthew Wilson said the cancer had spread.

Caen, a flamboyant, larger-than-life character, wrote a daily column for 58 years, longer than anyone in the history of American newspapers. He was an institution in San Francisco, where he had a huge following.

President Clinton and his wife Hillary expressed sadness at Caen's death and said his "witty, irrepressible voice" would be missed. "...Surely no one knew better the vibrancy and eccentricities of The City, his city, San Francisco, than did Herb Caen," Clinton said in a statement.
"We are deeply saddened by Herb's death. Our hearts go out to his wife and family, and his millions of fans," San Francisco Chronicle Editor Bill German said.
San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown, a close friend of Caen, ordered flags in the city flown at half-staff in his honour.

Brown, who joined Chronicle editors in the paper's newsroom to pay tribute to the columnist, said Caen "interpreted the city and gave you a picture of the city that was in your head but you could never articulate."

When he last spoke with Caen in January, Brown said, the columnist was flat on his back receiving cancer treatment. But Caen did not dwell on his condition and was only interested in Brown giving him an "item" for his column, Brown said.
"He was still being a newsman no matter what and I think he probably expired this morning being a newsman," he said.
Brown said some public figures prefered a nasty mention in Caen's column to an approving one on the editorial page.
Wilson said the Chronicle had no plans to replace Caen. "It can't be done," Wilson said.

Caen, who was born in Sacramento, California on April 3, 1916, began writing a daily column in the San Francisco Chronicle about city life July 5, 1938. Except for service overseas during World War II and a period with the rival San Francisco Examiner during the 1950s, Caen wrote the daily column for the Chronicle until recently.

In nearly 16,000 columns, Caen chronicled the changing panorama of San Francisco, the city he loved. The columns included short items of news, gossip, amusing anecdotes and observations, all joined by his trademark three dots, a technique borrowed from famous columnist Walter Winchell. He was also fond of puns and coining words.

Caen was famous for his hard-charging lifestyle. He pounded out his column on his trusty "Royal" typewriter by day and frequented clubs and bars by night, perpetually in search of more "items" for his column. Usually wearing a suit and fedora, he was partial to vodka, which he called "vitamin V".

For decades, he produced the column six days a week, only cutting back to five a week in 1991. Despite arduous cancer treatment since last year, Caen continued to write from time to time and his last column appeared on Jan. 10.

A week after Caen turned 80 last April, the Pulitzer Board awarded him a special prize for his "extraordinary and continuing contribution as a voice and conscience of his city." He also married for the fourth time, to long-time companion Ann Moller. His three earlier marriages ended in divorce.

San Francisco threw a huge party for Caen last June, when a new bayside promenade named "Herb Caen Way" was dedicated. Actors Robin Williams and Don Johnson were among the 75,000 people who turned out to honour Caen.
Caen is survived by his wife Ann and his son Christopher.
